title: Syncope Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for syncope (transient loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion) in adults, covering reflex, orthostatic, and cardiac etiologies per the ESC 2018 classification.
source_description: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, et al. Eur Heart J 2018;39(21):1883-1948.

diagnoses.name: Cardiac Arrhythmia (Bradycardia or Tachycardia)
key_features: Syncope during exertion or supine
Sudden onset without prodrome
Palpitations preceding syncope
Family history of sudden cardiac death
Known structural heart disease
red_flags: ECG showing bifascicular block, QTc >460 ms, Brugada pattern, or pre-excitation
Sinus bradycardia <40 bpm or sinus pauses >3 seconds while awake

diagnoses.name: Structural Cardiac or Cardiopulmonary Disease
key_features: Syncope during exertion
Known severe aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
New-onset dyspnea with syncope
Unilateral leg swelling suggesting DVT/PE
red_flags: Syncope with exertion in patient with known structural heart disease
Signs of acute pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection
recommended_tests: CT pulmonary angiography if PE suspected

diagnoses.name: Vasovagal Syncope
key_features: Provoked by prolonged standing, pain, emotional distress, or blood phobia
Prodrome of lightheadedness, warmth, nausea, diaphoresis, pallor
Rapid recovery after assuming supine position
Associated with crowded or warm environments
recommended_tests: Clinical history and examination often sufficient
Tilt-table testing if recurrent and diagnosis uncertain

diagnoses.name: Situational Syncope
key_features: Syncope triggered by specific situations: micturition, defecation, coughing, swallowing, post-exercise
Reproducible association with the triggering activity
May have prodromal symptoms similar to vasovagal syncope

diagnoses.name: Carotid Sinus Syncope
key_features: Syncope associated with head turning, tight collars, or neck pressure
Typically in patients over 40 years old
Abnormal cardioinhibition (asystole >=3 seconds) or vasodepression (systolic BP drop >50 mmHg) on carotid sinus massage
recommended_tests: Carotid sinus massage (in patients >40 years with unexplained syncope)
Carotid duplex to exclude significant stenosis before massage

diagnoses.name: Orthostatic Hypotension (Drug-Induced or Volume Depletion)
key_features: Syncope occurs on standing or shortly after standing
Use of vasodilators, diuretics, antidepressants, or alpha-blockers
Volume depletion from hemorrhage, diarrhea, vomiting, or poor intake
Systolic BP drop >=20 mmHg or diastolic >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing
red_flags: Severe dehydration with altered mental status
recommended_tests: Active standing test with BP measurement at 1 and 3 minutes
Complete blood count if hemorrhage suspected

diagnoses.name: Autonomic Failure (Primary or Secondary)
key_features: Recurrent syncope with orthostatic hypotension not explained by drugs or volume depletion
Associated with Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, or diabetic neuropathy
Progressive autonomic symptoms including anhidrosis, bladder dysfunction, gastroparesis
Supine hypertension with standing hypotension
red_flags: New neurological symptoms suggesting neurodegenerative disease
recommended_tests: Deep breathing heart rate variability test

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Embolism
key_features: Syncope as presenting symptom of massive or submassive PE
Acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia
Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilization, malignancy, oral contraceptives
Unilateral leg swelling
red_flags: Syncope is the presenting symptom in approximately 10% of PE cases

also_consider.name: Epileptic Seizure
also_consider.rationale: Key differential of TLOC; distinguished by tonic-clonic movements, tongue biting, postictal confusion >5 minutes, and cyanosis during episode

also_consider.name: Psychogenic Pseudosyncope (PNES)
also_consider.rationale: Prolonged apparent LOC (minutes vs seconds in true syncope), eyes often closed, high frequency of episodes, no hemodynamic changes on tilt testing

also_consider.name: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS)
also_consider.rationale: Heart rate increase >30 bpm or >120 bpm on standing without significant BP drop; predominant in young women with presyncope, fatigue, and palpitations

also_consider.name: Subclavian Steal Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Syncope with arm exercise; vertebrobasilar insufficiency from proximal subclavian artery stenosis; check bilateral arm BP

also_consider.name: Vertebrobasilar TIA
also_consider.rationale: Transient loss of consciousness with brainstem symptoms (diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo); isolated syncope without focal neurological signs is rarely TIA

also_consider.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
also_consider.rationale: Sudden severe headache (thunderclap) with transient LOC; must be excluded in syncope with headache

also_consider.name: Hypoglycemia
also_consider.rationale: Altered consciousness in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas; typically gradual onset with diaphoresis, tremor, confusion rather than abrupt syncope

also_consider.name: Aortic Dissection
also_consider.rationale: Syncope in 5-10% of dissections; suspect with tearing chest/back pain and blood pressure differential between arms

also_consider.name: Cardiac Tamponade
also_consider.rationale: Syncope from impaired cardiac filling; consider in patients with pericardial effusion, malignancy, or recent cardiac procedure

also_consider.name: Atrial Myxoma
also_consider.rationale: Positional syncope from intermittent obstruction of mitral valve; rare but classic cause of positional syncope with a cardiac tumor plop on auscultation

also_consider.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction
also_consider.rationale: Syncope in 3-5% of MI presentations; may be due to arrhythmia or reflex mechanism; always obtain ECG in syncope evaluation

also_consider.name: Medication-Induced QT Prolongation
also_consider.rationale: Drug-induced torsades de pointes causing syncope; review medications including antiarrhythmics, antibiotics, and psychotropics for QT-prolonging potential

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set derived from the ESC 2018 Syncope Guidelines, not an exhaustive differential. Syncope evaluation must begin with a thorough initial assessment including detailed history, physical examination with orthostatic vitals, and 12-lead ECG. The ESC risk stratification distinguishes high-risk patients (suggesting cardiac syncope with higher mortality risk) from low-risk patients (suggesting reflex syncope with benign prognosis). Always consider atypical presentations, medication effects, and non-syncopal causes of transient loss of consciousness (epilepsy, psychogenic). In elderly patients, multifactorial causes are common.
